interactions.label: A 40-year-old woman presents with menorrhagia and a firm, irregular pelvic mass.

params.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with menorrhagia and a firm, irregular pelvic mass. On bimanual examination, which finding would most strongly suggest the mass is a fibroid uterus rather than an ovarian tumour?

answers.text: The mass is non-tender on palpation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-tenderness is common in both fibroids and many ovarian tumours, so it does not reliably distinguish the two.

answers.text: The mass moves together with the cervix

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A fibroid is part of the uterine body, so it moves with the cervix on bimanual palpation — this hallmark finding distinguishes it from an ovarian mass, which moves independently.

answers.text: The mass is palpable in the suprapubic region

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both a large fibroid and a large ovarian tumour can be palpable suprapubically; this finding alone does not distinguish between them.

answers.text: The mass has irregular margins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While fibroids often feel irregular, some ovarian tumours can also be irregular. The bimanual relationship with the cervix is the more reliable distinguishing sign.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key finding is that a fibroid uterus moves together with the cervix on bimanual palpation, because the fibroid is continuous with the uterine body. An ovarian mass moves independently of the cervix.
Well done! A uterine fibroid moves with the cervix because it is part of the uterine body — this is the key bimanual finding distinguishing it from an ovarian mass.

interactions.label: Which of the following best distinguishes adenomyosis from endometriosis on clin

params.question: Which of the following best distinguishes adenomyosis from endometriosis on clinical examination?

answers.text: Adenomyosis causes deep dyspareunia, while endometriosis does not

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deep dyspareunia is actually a hallmark of endometriosis (from deposits in the Pouch of Douglas and uterosacral ligaments), not of adenomyosis.

answers.text: In adenomyosis the uterus is uniformly enlarged and boggy; in endometriosis it may be fixed but is not enlarged

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Adenomyosis causes symmetrical, boggy uterine enlargement because endometrial tissue infiltrates the myometrium. In endometriosis, the uterus is usually normal-sized but may be fixed and retroverted due to pelvic adhesions.

answers.text: In endometriosis the uterus is irregularly enlarged; in adenomyosis it is normal-sized

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is reversed. In endometriosis, the uterus is typically not enlarged; in adenomyosis, it is uniformly enlarged. An irregularly enlarged uterus suggests fibroids, not endometriosis.

answers.text: Endometriosis causes menorrhagia as its dominant symptom, while adenomyosis presents mainly with pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the opposite of the actual pattern. Pain (dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia) dominates in endometriosis, while heavy menstrual bleeding dominates in adenomyosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: in adenomyosis the uterus is uniformly enlarged, soft, and boggy (bleeding dominates); in endometriosis the uterus may be fixed by adhesions but is not enlarged (pain dominates).
Excellent! Adenomyosis = uniformly boggy enlarged uterus with bleeding as the dominant symptom. Endometriosis = normal-sized but possibly fixed uterus with pain as the dominant symptom.

params.question: In uterine prolapse, urinary symptoms such as stress incontinence and difficulty voiding are caused by descent of the posterior vaginal wall.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Urinary symptoms are caused by the cystocele — descent of the anterior vaginal wall carrying the bladder base — not the posterior wall. Posterior wall descent (rectocele) is associated with bowel symptoms like constipation and the need for digital support to evacuate.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Urinary symptoms in prolapse result from descent of the anterior vaginal wall (cystocele), which displaces the bladder base and kinks the urethra. The posterior wall (rectocele) causes bowel symptoms such as constipation and incomplete evacuation.

params.question: A 36-year-old woman has had no periods for 14 months and is diagnosed with premature ovarian insufficiency. Which statement regarding her management is most accurate?

answers.text: Hormone replacement therapy is contraindicated at her age due to thrombotic risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HRT is not contraindicated in premature ovarian insufficiency. These women need HRT precisely because early oestrogen loss places them at significantly higher risk of osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease.

answers.text: Hormone replacement therapy should be continued at least until the natural age of menopause, around 50 years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Women with premature ovarian insufficiency face accelerated bone loss and cardiovascular risk due to early oestrogen depletion. HRT replaces the hormones the ovaries would have produced until the natural menopause age (~50 years).

answers.text: No treatment is needed unless she develops vasomotor symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HRT in premature ovarian insufficiency is not just for symptom relief. The main reason is to protect against long-term complications — osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease — regardless of whether hot flushes are present.

answers.text: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone is sufficient to manage her long-term risks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While bone health supplements are important, they do not address the cardiovascular risk or the broader effects of premature oestrogen deficiency. HRT remains the recommended treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: In premature ovarian insufficiency, HRT is recommended until at least the natural age of menopause (~50 years). The early loss of ovarian oestrogen significantly increases long-term risk of osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease.
Correct! In premature ovarian insufficiency, HRT is continued until at least the natural menopause age (~50) to protect against osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease from early oestrogen loss.

interactions.label: Post-menopausal bleeding mandates urgent investigation in every case, regardless

params.question: Post-menopausal bleeding mandates urgent investigation in every case, regardless of the amount of bleeding. Which of the following best justifies this clinical policy?

answers.text: Atrophic vaginitis, the commonest cause, cannot be distinguished from malignancy without histology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While histology may sometimes be needed, clinical and ultrasound assessment can often suggest atrophic vaginitis. The reason for universal investigation is the unacceptably high prevalence of carcinoma, not the inability to diagnose atrophy.

answers.text: Approximately 10% of women presenting with post-menopausal bleeding are found to have endometrial carcinoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A 10% prevalence of endometrial carcinoma among women with PMB is high enough that no case can safely be dismissed. Even minimal spotting may be the presenting feature of carcinoma, while heavy bleeding may be benign.

answers.text: The volume of post-menopausal bleeding directly correlates with the severity of the underlying pathology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is precisely the dangerous assumption the video warns against. Bleeding amount does not predict severity — scanty spotting can be carcinoma, while heavy bleeding may be from a benign polyp or atrophic endometrium.

answers.text: Cervical carcinoma is the most common malignant cause of post-menopausal bleeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Endometrial carcinoma, not cervical carcinoma, is the primary malignant concern in post-menopausal bleeding. The 10% prevalence of endometrial carcinoma is the figure that drives the mandatory investigation policy.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key figure is 10% — approximately one in ten women with post-menopausal bleeding has endometrial carcinoma. This prevalence justifies mandatory investigation of every case, no matter how small the bleed.
Excellent! The ~10% prevalence of endometrial carcinoma among women with PMB justifies urgent investigation in every case, regardless of the amount of bleeding.

interactions.label: A 32-year-old nulliparous woman with a 6 cm intramural fibroid and menorrhagia w

params.question: A 32-year-old nulliparous woman with a 6 cm intramural fibroid and menorrhagia wishes to conceive in the near future. Which management plan is most appropriate?

answers.text: Hysterectomy, as it is the only curative option and prevents recurrence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hysterectomy removes the uterus entirely, making future pregnancy impossible. It is reserved for women who have completed their families and desire definitive treatment.

answers.text: Uterine artery embolisation to shrink the fibroid without surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Uterine artery embolisation is generally not recommended for women planning pregnancy, as it may compromise uterine blood supply and adversely affect fertility and pregnancy outcomes.

answers.text: GnRH agonist for 3 months followed by myomectomy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A GnRH agonist creates a temporary low-oestrogen state that shrinks the fibroid by 35–60%, reducing blood loss and surgical difficulty. Myomectomy then removes the fibroid while preserving the uterus for future conception.

answers.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (Mirena) as definitive treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Mirena IUS can reduce menstrual bleeding from smaller fibroids but does not shrink or remove the fibroid. It is not suitable when large fibroids distort the cavity, and it is not definitive treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: For a woman wishing to preserve fertility, the appropriate plan is a GnRH agonist for 3 months (to shrink the fibroid by 35–60%) followed by myomectomy, which removes the fibroid while keeping the uterus intact.
Well done! For a young woman wanting to conceive, GnRH agonist pre-treatment followed by myomectomy is the standard fertility-preserving approach for significant fibroids.
